groups.title: Sensing & mediators
groups.question: How is danger recognised and communicated?

groups.title: Immune cells
groups.question: Which cells recognise, respond and cooperate?

groups.title: Regulation & repair
groups.question: What restrains injury and shapes recovery?

groups.title: Clinical phenotypes
groups.question: Which mechanism fits this clinical context?

groups.title: Organ interfaces
groups.question: Which connections are supported by evidence?

groups.title: Observation & translation
groups.question: How do we observe, test and translate a claim?

topics.title: Pattern recognition
topics.idea: Pattern-recognition receptors detect microbial structures and damage-associated signals in immune and cardiac-resident cells. Their signalling initiates context-dependent innate responses.
topics.heart: TLRs, cytosolic nucleic-acid sensors and downstream pathways connect infection or sterile injury to inflammatory activation.
topics.evidence: Receptor expression is not proof of pathway activation. Viral and sterile injury can share sensors while requiring different interpretations.
topics.question: What is being sensed: a pathogen, damaged tissue, or both?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Complement
topics.idea: A regulated protein cascade: classical, lectin and alternative activation converge on C3. Opsonisation, inflammatory signalling and the terminal complex are key outputs.
topics.heart: Connects host defence with tissue injury; cardiovascular research includes ischaemia–reperfusion and vascular inflammation.
topics.evidence: Mechanistic involvement does not establish benefit from complement inhibition in every cardiac disease.
topics.question: Which pathway, fragment and disease stage are implicated?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Inflammasome
topics.idea: Intracellular protein complexes that can activate caspase-1 and promote maturation of IL-1β and IL-18.
topics.heart: A bridge between cellular danger signals and inflammatory pathways studied in cardiovascular injury.
topics.evidence: Distinguish evidence about a specific inflammasome from evidence about its downstream cytokines.
topics.question: Is the evidence about inflammasome assembly, a cytokine, or pyroptosis?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Cytokine networks
topics.idea: Cytokines form context-dependent networks between immune, vascular and stromal cells. IL-1, IL-6 and other interleukins have distinct sources, receptors and effects.
topics.heart: Cytokine inhibition tests a specific target in a defined population; it does not test all inflammation at once.
topics.evidence: A fall in CRP or another biomarker does not establish a reduction in cardiovascular events.
topics.question: Which ligand, receptor and patient population are being studied?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Immunometabolism
topics.idea: The interaction between metabolic state and immune-cell function.
topics.heart: Helps frame inflammatory responses to ischaemic injury and cardiometabolic stress.
topics.evidence: A promising translational field; changing a cellular metabolic pathway is not automatically a validated therapy.
topics.question: Is altered metabolism driving cell function, reflecting injury, or both?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Gut–heart axis
topics.idea: Microbial communities and their metabolites interact with host physiology and immunity.
topics.heart: The gut–heart axis connects diet, microbial metabolism and cardiovascular phenotypes.
topics.evidence: A prospective association or a predictive model does not show that changing the microbiome prevents cardiovascular disease.
topics.question: Does the study show association, prediction or a causal intervention?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Cardiac macrophages
topics.idea: Resident and recruited macrophage populations participate in surveillance, clearance and repair. Ontogeny, tissue niche and activation state all matter; a simple M1/M2 split is insufficient.
topics.heart: Cardiac macrophages interact with cardiomyocytes, vessels and fibroblasts. Their roles vary between homeostasis, acute injury and chronic disease.
topics.evidence: Much mechanistic evidence comes from models; origin alone does not fully define a cell’s function.
topics.question: Which origin, state, niche and time after injury?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits
topics.terms: macrophages monocytes résidents recrutés moelle CCR2 ontogénie état niche temporalité M1 M2

topics.title: T lymphocytes
topics.idea: T cells support antigen-specific effector, memory and regulatory responses. CD4, CD8, regulatory and unconventional populations differ in their receptors, state and tissue functions.
topics.heart: Antigen specificity distinguishes targeted cardiac immune responses from a nonspecific inflammatory infiltrate.
topics.evidence: Cell identity, activation state and tissue context matter; “lymphocyte” is not one uniform mechanism.
topics.question: Which subset, antigen specificity and tissue compartment?
topics.terms: lymphocytes T CD4 CD8 Treg Th1 Th2 Th17 Tfh gamma delta MAIT mémoire cytotoxicité
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Dendritic cells
topics.question: Which dendritic-cell subset, maturation state and antigen?
topics.idea: Dendritic cells integrate danger sensing, antigen processing and T-cell priming. Their subset, maturation state and tissue niche influence immunity or tolerance.
topics.heart: Cardiac antigen sampling and presentation provide a bridge between local tissue injury, draining lymph nodes and adaptive responses.
topics.evidence: Conventional and plasmacytoid subsets have different functions. Benefits of engineered cells in experimental models do not establish a clinical treatment.
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Neutrophils & NETs
topics.question: Which neutrophil state and which evidence of NET formation?
topics.idea: Neutrophils coordinate antimicrobial defence, acute inflammation and interactions with platelets and other immune cells. Extracellular traps are one effector mechanism, not a synonym for all neutrophil activity.
topics.heart: NET-associated processes connect thrombosis, reperfusion injury and repair, while timing and tissue context shape the effects of neutrophils.
topics.evidence: Circulating NET-associated markers do not uniquely identify tissue NET formation or show that NET-directed treatment improves clinical outcomes.
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Antigen presentation
topics.idea: Antigen-presenting cells process proteins and display peptides to T cells. Dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells differ in how they prime, sustain or regulate responses.
topics.heart: Presentation of cardiac antigens links tissue injury to T-cell activation or tolerance. Antigen release alone is not evidence of pathogenic autoimmunity.
topics.evidence: Distinguish antigen presentation, demonstrable antigen-specific responses and proof that those responses cause disease.
topics.question: Who presents which antigen, through which MHC and co-signals?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Immune tolerance
topics.idea: Mechanisms that prevent or restrain immune responses against self. Central selection and peripheral control are complementary safeguards.
topics.heart: A conceptual bridge to autoimmune disease, graft rejection and adverse effects of immune therapies.
topics.evidence: Tolerance is not simply the absence of inflammation or general immunosuppression.
topics.question: Which protective control is lost, preserved or being restored?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Resolution
topics.idea: Active containment and ending of an inflammatory response, rather than merely a fall in inflammatory markers.
topics.heart: Timely resolution and clearance of the infiltrate are important for organised cardiac repair.
topics.evidence: Stopping inflammation and restoring functional tissue are related but different outcomes.
topics.question: Has inflammation resolved, and has tissue function recovered?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Remodeling
topics.idea: Changes in cardiac structure and function after injury or persistent stress.
topics.heart: Inflammatory and reparative responses contribute to the trajectory after myocardial injury.
topics.evidence: Remodelling describes a process; it is not synonymous with inflammation or proof of its cause.
topics.question: Which structural change, at which phase after injury?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Fibrosis
topics.idea: Accumulation and reorganisation of extracellular matrix, including scar formation after tissue loss.
topics.heart: A scar can preserve integrity, while persistent or diffuse fibrosis may impair function.
topics.evidence: Active fibroblast signalling, accumulated scar and potential reversibility are different quantities. An imaging signal needs validation against the biological process it is claimed to measure.
topics.question: Active fibroblast signalling, matrix deposition or established scar?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Regeneration
topics.idea: Replacement of lost functional tissue; distinct from repair by scar formation.
topics.heart: Experimental cardiac repair studies investigate how inflammatory and stromal responses affect recovery.
topics.evidence: Results in mice do not establish restoration of human myocardium or a ready-to-use treatment.
topics.question: Is functional myocardium replaced, or is scar formation modified?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Atherosclerosis
topics.idea: Arterial plaque disease in which lipids and inflammatory processes interact.
topics.heart: A major cardiovascular setting for studying the consequences of immune activation.
topics.evidence: Inflammation is one component of risk, alongside other established contributors.
topics.question: Does target engagement translate into fewer clinical events?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Pericarditis
topics.idea: Inflammation of the pericardium, the sac surrounding the heart.
topics.heart: Shows why anatomical site, disease course and cause should be considered separately.
topics.evidence: Clinical assessment and disease-specific guidance are needed; a pathway alone does not define management.
topics.question: Which cause, inflammatory phenotype and recurrence pattern?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Myocarditis
topics.idea: Inflammation involving the heart muscle.
topics.heart: Distinct from pericarditis, although the two may overlap.
topics.evidence: The cause, clinical presentation and evidence of tissue injury need individual assessment.
topics.question: What establishes inflammation, its cause and the risk profile?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Sarcoidosis
topics.idea: A multisystem disease characterised by granulomatous inflammation.
topics.heart: Cardiac involvement is a distinct concern within a disease that may affect several organs.
topics.evidence: A diagnosis in one organ does not by itself define the presence or severity of cardiac involvement.
topics.question: Active inflammation, scar, or a combination of both?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Amyloidosis
topics.idea: Misfolded proteins accumulate in tissue. Cardiac AL amyloidosis and transthyretin amyloidosis are biologically distinct entities.
topics.heart: Included at the boundary of the map: AL involves an immunoglobulin-producing clone, whereas ATTR is not primarily an immune-mediated myocarditis.
topics.evidence: AL and transthyretin amyloidosis are distinct; infiltration must not be equated with active immune inflammation.
topics.question: Which amyloid protein is demonstrated?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Systemic diseases
topics.idea: Immune-mediated diseases may involve several organs rather than one isolated tissue.
topics.heart: Lupus, for example, can involve the heart as well as other organs.
topics.evidence: Mechanisms and organ patterns differ between diseases; extrapolation requires care.
topics.question: What is established in the heart, rather than inferred from another organ?
topics.terms: lupus sclérodermie myosite Sjögren polyarthrite autoimmunité systémique connective tissue disease
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Vasculitis
topics.idea: Inflammation affecting blood vessels, with manifestations depending on the vessels and organs involved.
topics.heart: Connects vascular injury with questions about the heart and other organs.
topics.evidence: The vasculitis subtype matters; a general label does not determine a patient’s organ involvement.
topics.question: Which subtype, vessel size, activity and cardiac manifestation?
topics.terms: vascularites ANCA GPA MPA EGPA Behçet Kawasaki petits moyens gros vaisseaux
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Autoinflammation
topics.idea: Disorders characterised by inappropriate activation of innate inflammatory pathways.
topics.heart: Offers a framework for understanding recurrent inflammatory syndromes and their interfaces.
topics.evidence: Autoinflammation and autoimmunity overlap in some settings but are not interchangeable terms.
topics.question: What supports an autoinflammatory rather than an infectious or autoimmune mechanism?
topics.terms: auto-inflammation FMF TRAPS CAPS Still fièvre périodique IL-1
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Pulmonary hypertension
topics.idea: Elevated pressure in the pulmonary circulation, arising through different disease groups.
topics.heart: Connects pulmonary vascular disease with the workload of the right heart.
topics.evidence: The underlying group and cause matter; inflammation is not the sole explanation for pulmonary hypertension.
topics.question: Which haemodynamic group, and what evidence of immune involvement?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Heart failure & cardiomyopathy
topics.idea: A clinical syndrome with multiple possible causes.
topics.heart: Provides a shared clinical outcome in which vascular, myocardial and systemic processes may converge.
topics.evidence: Heart failure is not one immune disease; identifying a mechanism requires more than the syndrome label.
topics.question: Which cause and phenotype explain the immune signal?
topics.terms: insuffisance cardiaque HFpEF HFrEF cardiomyopathie dilatée DCM ACM génétique péripartum diabète obésité sexes ventricule droit oreillette
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Cardio-oncology
topics.idea: The cardiovascular consequences of cancer and its treatments.
topics.heart: Immune therapies are an important interface, alongside other cancer-related cardiovascular effects.
topics.evidence: Risk and management depend on the treatment and clinical setting; mechanisms cannot be generalised across agents.
topics.question: Which therapy, immune lesion and competing diagnosis?
topics.terms: ICI inhibiteurs checkpoints immunitaires CAR-T syndrome libération cytokines CRS cancer radiothérapie toxicité immunothérapie
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Cardio-infectiology
topics.idea: The cardiovascular interfaces of infection, including infective endocarditis.
topics.heart: Connects pathogen, host response and cardiac tissue or device involvement.
topics.evidence: The selected influenza study combines human observations with mechanistic animal work. It does not explain every infection-related cardiac syndrome.
topics.question: What distinguishes pathogen persistence from immune-mediated damage?
topics.terms: infection virus influenza SARS-CoV-2 VIH Chagas endocardite sepsis post-infectieux
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Transplantation
topics.idea: Replacement of a failing heart with a donor organ, with continuing attention to immune rejection.
topics.heart: Makes recognition of non-self and its regulation clinically tangible.
topics.evidence: Rejection, infection and graft dysfunction are distinct problems requiring specialist evaluation.
topics.question: Cellular rejection, antibody-mediated injury, infection or another graft problem?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Ocular immunity
topics.idea: Immune-mediated and infectious inflammation of the eye; uveitis is one example.
topics.heart: A cross-organ perspective for reading multisystem inflammation, rather than a claim of a universal eye–heart mechanism.
topics.evidence: An inflammatory sign in the eye does not establish a cardiac diagnosis.
topics.question: Which ocular mechanism is demonstrated, and can it be extrapolated?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Renal immunity
topics.idea: Immune injury in the kidney, illustrated by lupus nephritis.
topics.heart: Offers a cross-organ way to think about systemic disease and organ-specific damage.
topics.evidence: The selected human study identifies signatures in lupus nephritis. Its findings cannot diagnose cardiac involvement or establish a cardiac therapeutic target.
topics.question: Do circulating signatures reflect kidney injury, cardiac injury or systemic activity?
topics.terms: rein rénal néphrite cardiorénal lupus complément urémie
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Neuroimmune axis
topics.idea: Interactions between immunity and the nervous system; multiple sclerosis is a familiar example of immune-mediated damage.
topics.heart: Included as a neighbouring discipline for comparing tissue context and organ vulnerability.
topics.evidence: This conceptual connection does not imply a common cardiac mechanism or treatment.
topics.question: Which neural circuit, immune effector and cardiac outcome are linked?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Pulmonary immunity
topics.idea: Immune processes in the lung, including granulomatous inflammation in sarcoidosis.
topics.heart: Connects a multisystem perspective with pulmonary and cardiovascular questions.
topics.evidence: Shared inflammatory vocabulary does not mean identical organ behaviour.
topics.question: Is cardiac stress secondary to pulmonary vascular disease or direct cardiac involvement?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Cardio-rheumatology
topics.idea: Systemic immune-mediated diseases may involve joints, skin and internal organs.
topics.heart: Lupus illustrates why cardiovascular questions belong within a wider organ assessment.
topics.evidence: Troponin indicates myocardial injury in context; assay interference and non-inflammatory causes must also be considered.
topics.question: Inflammatory injury, vascular disease, treatment effect or an analytical interference?
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Clonal haematopoiesis
topics.question: Which driver mutation, clone size and clinical endpoint?
topics.idea: Somatic mutations can expand a haematopoietic clone and alter the inflammatory behaviour of its blood-cell descendants. Different driver genes do not produce one uniform immune phenotype.
topics.heart: Clonal haematopoiesis links ageing, myeloid biology and cardiovascular risk, including atherosclerosis and heart failure.
topics.evidence: Risk associations and mechanistic models do not establish routine population screening or a validated clone-directed cardiovascular treatment.
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Chemokines & trafficking
topics.question: Which cell is recruited, through which receptor and into which compartment?
topics.idea: Chemokine gradients and adhesion signals position immune cells within tissues. Expression, migration and retention are distinct observations.
topics.heart: CCL2–CCR2 and CXCL-family pathways help frame the recruitment of myeloid and lymphoid cells to injured myocardium.
topics.evidence: Chemokine abundance alone cannot identify its cellular source, demonstrate a functional gradient or establish benefit from receptor blockade.
topics.terms: chimiokines recrutement migration adhésion CCL2 CCR2 CXCL9 CXCL10 CXCR3
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Autoantibodies
topics.question: Does the antibody bind, alter function, or cause disease?
topics.idea: Autoantibodies may bind cardiac antigens or influence receptor signalling. Their presence and their functional effects need separate assays.
topics.heart: Humoral mechanisms are studied in myocardial disease, systemic autoimmunity and graft injury.
topics.evidence: Association, functional activity and pathogenic causality are different claims. A positive antibody test does not by itself justify immune therapy.
topics.terms: autoanticorps autoimmunité humorale immunoglobulines récepteurs complexes immuns Fc
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Trained immunity
topics.question: Which earlier exposure leaves which durable change?
topics.idea: Some innate cells and their progenitors retain altered responsiveness after an earlier stimulus through metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming.
topics.heart: Persistent myeloid responses provide a framework for studying vascular inflammation after metabolic or infectious exposures.
topics.evidence: This is not antigen-specific adaptive memory. Demonstrating a chromatin signature alone does not establish a clinically useful intervention.
topics.terms: immunité entraînée mémoire innée épigénétique tolérance innée moelle progéniteurs
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: B cells & plasma cells
topics.question: Which B-cell state, specificity and function are implicated?
topics.idea: B cells can present antigen and produce cytokines; differentiated plasma cells secrete antibodies. Regulatory and effector functions depend on state and context.
topics.heart: B-cell responses and receptor repertoires are studied in myocarditis and other cardiac immune settings.
topics.evidence: B-cell depletion and suppression of long-lived plasma cells are not equivalent. Findings in experimental myocarditis do not establish a broadly effective cardiac treatment.
topics.terms: lymphocytes B plasmocytes BCR Breg mémoire centres germinatifs
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: NK cells & ILCs
topics.question: Which lineage, activation state and target are being examined?
topics.idea: Natural killer cells and helper innate lymphoid populations differ in cytotoxicity and cytokine programmes. They lack the rearranged antigen receptors of conventional B and T cells.
topics.heart: These populations participate in experimental responses to infection, injury and tissue repair in the heart.
topics.evidence: NK, NKT and ILC subsets should not be conflated. A circulating cell count cannot establish the function of a tissue-resident population.
topics.terms: cellules NK lymphoïdes innées ILC1 ILC2 ILC3 NKT cytotoxicité perforine granzymes
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Eosinophils
topics.question: Which cause and which evidence of eosinophilic tissue injury?
topics.idea: Eosinophils release granule proteins and lipid mediators. Blood eosinophilia and eosinophilic myocardial infiltration describe different findings.
topics.heart: Hypersensitivity, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis and hypereosinophilic disorders can be associated with cardiac injury.
topics.evidence: A normal blood count does not exclude tissue disease. Imaging can suggest a phenotype but cannot by itself establish its histological cause.
topics.terms: éosinophiles EGPA hyperéosinophilie hypersensibilité myocardite éosinophilique
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Mast cells
topics.question: Which mediator and which phase of the response?
topics.idea: Mast cells are tissue-resident immune cells with granule-derived mediators, cytokines and proteases. Their functions vary across local environments.
topics.heart: Experimental work links cardiac mast cells to vascular responses, matrix remodelling and inflammatory regulation.
topics.evidence: Many functional claims remain preclinical. Cell abundance, degranulation and the effect of a particular mediator require different measurements.
topics.terms: mastocytes histamine tryptase chymase allergie Kounis basophiles
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Platelets
topics.question: Which platelet activity links haemostasis to immunity?
topics.idea: Platelets are anucleate blood elements that combine haemostatic functions with mediator release and interactions with immune cells.
topics.heart: Platelet–leukocyte interactions provide a bridge between vascular injury, inflammation and thrombus formation.
topics.evidence: Platelet activation is not one uniform state. A circulating activation marker does not demonstrate a causal tissue interaction.
topics.terms: plaquettes agrégation thrombo-inflammation vésicules extracellulaires CD40L
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Endothelium
topics.question: Which vascular bed and which endothelial state?
topics.idea: Endothelial cells regulate barrier function, leucocyte recruitment and signals exchanged with their tissue environment.
topics.heart: Coronary and pulmonary microvascular states can influence the distribution and consequences of cardiac inflammation.
topics.evidence: An endothelial transcriptomic signature needs functional validation. The heart and lung do not share one uniform endothelial programme.
topics.terms: endothélium microcirculation glycocalyx perméabilité adhésion péricytes cellules musculaires lisses
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Cardiomyocytes
topics.question: Is the myocyte a sensor, a target, or both?
topics.idea: Cardiomyocytes respond to injury and can activate innate sensing, cytokine and regulated cell-death pathways. Their contractile role does not make them immunologically passive.
topics.heart: In viral myocarditis, direct infection and host-mediated injury can converge on the same cardiac cell.
topics.evidence: A pathogen signal or an inflammatory transcript is not enough to separate direct cytotoxicity from immune-mediated damage.
topics.terms: cardiomyocytes mitochondries stress réticulum autophagie cardiotoxicité
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Fibroblast niches
topics.question: Which fibroblast state and which local partners?
topics.idea: Cardiac fibroblasts maintain extracellular matrix and organise niches. Injury can change their inflammatory, reparative and matrix-producing programmes.
topics.heart: Their interactions with immune and myocardial cells connect tissue integrity, inflammatory positioning and fibrosis.
topics.evidence: A fibroblast marker or a predicted ligand–receptor pair does not establish a functional interaction. Reducing scar formation and restoring contractile tissue are different outcomes.
topics.terms: fibroblastes stroma niches matrice TGF bêta FAP mécanobiologie périvasculaire
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Cardiac lymphatics
topics.question: What leaves the tissue, and where does it go?
topics.idea: Lymphatic vessels drain interstitial fluid and support movement of immune cells and antigens towards lymph nodes.
topics.heart: Experimental myocardial injury studies connect lymphatic remodelling with inflammatory clearance and recovery.
topics.evidence: More lymphatic vessels do not automatically mean effective drainage. Translational benefit needs demonstration beyond vessel density in animal tissue.
topics.terms: lymphatiques ganglions drainage œdème circulation lymphatique lymphangiogenèse
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Efferocytosis
topics.question: Are dying cells recognised, engulfed and processed successfully?
topics.idea: Phagocytes clear apoptotic cells through coordinated recognition, engulfment and processing. Failed clearance can prolong local injury.
topics.heart: Efferocytosis helps frame resolution after myocardial infarction and clearance within atherosclerotic lesions.
topics.evidence: Increased phagocyte numbers do not establish efficient clearance. A mechanistic rescue in a model does not establish clinical efficacy.
topics.terms: efférocytose phagocytose MerTK CD47 apoptose eat-me clearance
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Cell death & danger
topics.question: Which death programme is demonstrated by which perturbation?
topics.idea: Apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis and ferroptosis describe distinct regulated processes. Their contributions can overlap in a diseased tissue.
topics.heart: Cell death changes myocardial cell mass and can release signals that recruit or activate immune responses.
topics.evidence: A single marker rarely identifies a unique death programme. PANoptosis describes proposed coordinated death circuitry and requires mechanistic evidence.
topics.terms: mort cellulaire apoptose nécroptose pyroptose ferroptose PANoptose DAMP
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Immune ageing
topics.question: How do age and senescence change the response?
topics.idea: Immune ageing and cellular senescence can alter surveillance, inflammatory tone and tissue repair. Chronological age does not fully capture these processes.
topics.heart: Senescent stromal, vascular and immune states are studied in age-associated cardiovascular dysfunction.
topics.evidence: A senescence-associated marker is not a complete cell identity. Senolytic findings in models do not establish routine human cardiac treatment.
topics.terms: vieillissement sénescence immunosénescence inflammaging SASP sexe genre hormones comorbidités
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Systemic hypertension
topics.question: What evidence supports immune involvement in this hypertensive setting?
topics.idea: Experimental and human studies examine immune pathways alongside vascular, renal and neurohumoral regulation of blood pressure.
topics.heart: Immune activation may contribute to vascular dysfunction and target-organ injury in selected contexts.
topics.evidence: Most hypertension is not established as an autoimmune disease. Immune associations do not replace validated blood-pressure management or establish benefit from immunosuppression.
topics.terms: hypertension artérielle HTA pression sodium angiotensine aldostérone
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Rhythm & conduction
topics.question: Which inflammatory process is linked to which electrical outcome?
topics.idea: Immune cells and inflammatory mediators can interact with electrical properties, tissue architecture and autonomic signals.
topics.heart: Atrial fibrillation, conduction disease and ventricular arrhythmia are different clinical settings; inflammation and scar may contribute in different ways.
topics.evidence: An inflammatory association does not prove an immune cause of an arrhythmia. Results in atrial fibrillation cannot be assumed to apply to every rhythm disorder.
topics.terms: arythmies fibrillation atriale conduction bloc ventriculaire mort subite
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Valvular disease
topics.question: Which valve process: post-infectious autoimmunity, calcification or another cause?
topics.idea: Rheumatic valve disease provides an established setting in which an immune response after infection can contribute to valve injury. Other valve diseases have different mechanisms.
topics.heart: Valve inflammation, fibrosis and calcification need to be distinguished from the haemodynamic consequence of a valve lesion.
topics.evidence: Not every valve lesion is immune-mediated. A review of rheumatic disease does not establish the mechanism of degenerative calcific disease.
topics.terms: valves valvulopathies rhumatisme articulaire aigu endocardite Libman Sacks calcification
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Aorta & large vessels
topics.question: Is the wall disease inflammatory, degenerative, genetic or mixed?
topics.idea: Large-vessel vasculitis and clinically isolated aortitis can affect aortic structure. Aneurysm is an anatomical finding with several possible causes.
topics.heart: Imaging, pathology and clinical context help separate active wall inflammation from established structural damage.
topics.evidence: A growth-rate association in an observational cohort does not prove treatment efficacy. Genetic and degenerative aneurysms must not be relabelled as autoimmune disease.
topics.terms: aorte aortite Takayasu artérite cellules géantes anévrisme dissection paroi
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Immunothrombosis & APS
topics.question: Which immune trigger contributes to which thrombotic event?
topics.idea: Coagulation, platelets, complement and immune cells can interact. Antiphospholipid syndrome is a specific autoimmune setting within this wider interface.
topics.heart: Arterial, venous and microvascular thrombosis have different contexts and consequences for the heart and circulation.
topics.evidence: An isolated antiphospholipid antibody result does not establish antiphospholipid syndrome. Classification criteria and individual clinical diagnosis serve different purposes.
topics.terms: immunothrombose SAPL antiphospholipides thrombose thromboembolie anticoagulation
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Cardiac imaging
topics.question: Which biological process does the image actually measure?
topics.idea: Echocardiography, magnetic resonance, CT and nuclear imaging measure different properties. Inflammation, extracellular expansion and active fibroblast signalling are not interchangeable signals.
topics.heart: Multimodality imaging can locate injury and follow ventricular, vascular or tissue consequences in an appropriate clinical context.
topics.evidence: An imaging pattern cannot automatically identify an immune cause. Molecular tracers require validation against the biological process they are claimed to measure.
topics.terms: imagerie échocardiographie IRM CMR TEP PET CT scanner strain LGE T1 T2 ECV
topics.evidenceLevel: Selected reading; see design and limits

topics.title: Biomarkers & sampling
topics.question: Which sample, assay, timing and clinical question?
topics.idea: A biomarker is interpreted through its biological source, analytical method and intended clinical use. Diagnostic, prognostic and treatment-response claims require different evidence.
topics.heart: Troponin, natriuretic peptides and inflammatory markers may inform complementary questions in cardiovascular disease.
topics.evidence: A biomarker may reflect processes outside the heart. A statistical association does not establish clinical utility or a treatment threshold.

topics.title: Single-cell & spatial
topics.question: Does proximity support a functional interaction?
topics.idea: Single-cell, single-nucleus and spatial methods describe cell states and their anatomical arrangement. Human cardiac atlases provide reference populations and niches.
topics.heart: These methods help formulate hypotheses about which immune, vascular and stromal cells may interact in the heart.
topics.evidence: Dissociation, sampling and computational choices can alter the result. Proximity and inferred ligand–receptor pairing do not establish causality; developmental and adult tissues are distinct.

topics.title: Causal evidence
topics.question: Which comparison would change the claim?
topics.idea: Perturbation experiments and randomised clinical comparisons answer different causal questions. Each requires a defined intervention, comparison, population and outcome.
topics.heart: Targeted IL-1β inhibition has been tested in selected patients with previous myocardial infarction and persistent inflammatory risk.
topics.evidence: A positive trial supports its tested intervention and setting, not every anti-inflammatory strategy. Bias, transportability, adverse events and absolute effects remain part of interpretation.

topics.title: Therapeutic translation
topics.question: Does target engagement improve a patient-relevant outcome?
topics.idea: Immune interventions differ in target, exposure, timing and consequences. Biomarker change and a reduction in clinical events are distinct outcomes.
topics.heart: Trials of colchicine after acute myocardial infarction and in chronic coronary disease illustrate why the clinical setting remains part of the claim.
topics.evidence: A neutral trial is not proof that immunity is irrelevant, and a positive trial does not validate all immune inhibition. Infection, toxicity and treatment interactions require separate assessment.
